items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
items.description:
I hope you had a fine

weekend. Mine was busy. For a while I briefly considered parting my hair on the side, but then discarded the idea. I also spent some time watching the dog for signs of listlessness, since I'd given him the new tranks. He was not listless. I wrote a lot, watched some interesting television programs, and, while studying the antecedents and source material of those retro-atomic AI videos we may or may not have discussed, realized that AI music makes me feel anxious and itchy. I'm talking about the mood-music / easy-listening "Luxury Jazz" that copies mid-century hi-fi swank. It's as if it sets the two hemispheres of the brain against each other. When I listened to an example of the real thing, it was like drinking fresh cold water after an hour of sucking on a paper towel soaked with Windex.

Lots of pursuits, in other words. I'm writing this on a Sunday night, ready for the chores and deadlines of the week to come, but man, am I glad that weekend is over. Saturdays are always bad. This one had a flavor of bad I haven't tasted since 1982. But that's for tomorrow. Now I give you what I wrote on Friday, with the now-traditional Old-Fashioned 11 PM Relaxation Writing Session. (Wedge of orange to garnish. Delicious.)

There are many good aspects

to this life. I can take a nap without guilt. I still set an alarm, though. Too much nap, and you drag. I get 6 and a half hours of sleep overnight, then 40 - 55 minutes between the utterly useless hour of 4 PM - 5 PM, and this keeps me reasonably sharp for evening work. The period after the nap feels cleanly demarcated from the time that went before. Everything resets - mood, energy, determination. Occasionally, though, it goes wrong. I jerked out of a nap because Iâd had an image in a dream that woke me up: a view of a glass in my hand slamming down on a table. It was one of my new glasses with the pebbled texture. There was something final and angry about the action, and I snapped away. Checked the clock: ehhhhhh. Iâd been out for 17 minutes.

But. Sometimes just entering REM is enough to recharge. I wondered if the glass-slam was my brainâs way of interpreting something else that jerked me awake. As I may have said, I nap wearingAirPods with white noise, and if Iâm dreaming when the alarm goes off, there is a moment where everyone falls silent and the action stops and everyone behaves with hushed confusion like a movie shoot after the director yells CUT out of nowhere. Silence, then the alarm. The brain rewrites the nap script the second the white noise cuts out.

Well, weâre up. Too early to start dinner. Donât want to sit at the computer and continue the day's rote work, which is renumbering the navigation for the 1930s B&W World site. Thereâs 12 minutes of daylight left. Letâs go for a walk.

I let him choose which direction: the old-style clockwise path that goes around Sunderwood, around the playground, then through Pentagon Park, or the Widdershins route. Today he chose the clockwise option. Halfway through he picked up an enormous stick and gave no sign of letting it go, and he trotted with the log half the distance back, course-correcting so he could deposit it at the auxiliary stick deposit spot.

This was the second stick of the day! O what luck! Post-gym we did the Centennial walk, and he dropped his stick to go say hello to the nice lady who works at FedEx, and sometimes just goes out the back door to stand there and bask in the sun. When we walked past she said âhello Birchâ so we went over to chat. Edinaâs Number One Dog.

Since it was Friday, I had pizza. Since the freezer compartment is small, there's no room for a frozen pizza, so Fridays I go to Target. Used to have four or five in the downstairs freezer, couple pep-saus for me, couple veg / pineapple for her, and I will go to my grave remembering the slight resistance of the freezer door when you pulled it, the big nail-and-screw organizer on the gray counter, the picture of a Texaco station leaning against the wall, the big COKE circle, the painting her mother did, the stack of neon-hued yardsticks piled up from years of the Fair shows. The very thought of "getting a pizza from the freezer" turns on the room in the mental holodeck. Joy. Anyway, got the pizza, and didn't mind the trip. Why, I had a Target Circle Deal: buy $30 worth of food, and get $5 off! Careful shopping got me enough food to last the rest of the week, but of course I will go grocery shopping.

Why? It gets me out, I suppose. Consumes time. You can talk to people and it's a great day when I can talk to someone.

Yes yes I should be out there signing up for improv classes or Adult Education or Pickleball or something, but thereâs the matter of the dog-shaped boat anchor chewing the leg of the entryway table the last time he was left alone.  I have new tranks to keep him from chewing through the pocket doors or madly scratching the walls looking for me, but they donât bring him down far enough. So if Iâm just going to hiber-hermit life going forward foreswearing the suburban bustle that occasionally produces Human Interaction, why not move to the distant lakeside town? I could join the historical society and hang out at the neighborhood pub.

I mean:  $265K.

You know what that gets you in the city? A rude shack in a part of town where the streets twinkle in the morn when the sun hits the broken car window glass and property taxes of 8K.

Hereâs something in the area Iâve been considering. It's one hundred and ten thousand dollars more than the house above.

I do not know what is going on with this kitchen:

Original ornamental wood over the sink. Probably the original door knobs. One metal sheet over the counters, stovetop controls to the left of the burners.

It has a shed.

If I go south to the river, the small town, I can have a proper office instead of a small bedroom with tiny rambler corner windows.

There are weeks when I think: yes yes of course, RICHFIELD! And there are weeks when it seems like that means living in a fargin' crackerbox at the periphery of the life I loved and lost.

And then there are nights like this, when I think: this year was a transition, and a good one. Familiar. The environs are connected to the old life but it wasnât anything we shared; this was always the Land of Errands. Instead of driving north to go home, now I go south. The Fred is a place through which people pass, each at a different pace. I stand on the balcony at night enjoying a lease violation and look at the lights, hear the constant white noise of the Seagate factory, and think: it was never forever. I was lucky that it was so different and interesting that it gave me a clear demarcation.

Staying around here is settling, sinking.

Leaving is . . . courageous?

Iâd make a rule: go up to the Cities on Wednesday and Sunday, see the lads.  Itâs only 87 minutes. It's ten minutes to Red Wing with a Target.

A porch. Summer. Crickets. The river a few blocks away.

Everything so different that I can settle into the rest of my days in proper exile.

Maybe thatâs what my dreams are telling me. The glass slams down on the table with a sharp rap.

Wake up.

In keeping with our Monday tradition, which became a "tradition" for reasons I can't recall and probably don't matter, we continue with our Monday trademark. For this year we'll do 1936.

The trademark for Republic Ictures:

They started up in 1935

, gathering all the Poverty Row studios into one brand. Republic would make over 1,000 movies before it closed in '67.

I'm always up for a good hell-noir:

Hey! Wow!

I had no idea! Okay, what do we have?

Let me just give you the basics of the first part, with a series of relevant frames.

We meet our protagonist, whoâs in his bed wearing a shirt and tie, with a cat.

The building's  seductive custodianess comes in and cleans the apartment.

He throws her out. Then he checks a piece of paper, and gets ready to go on a job.

He feeds the cat.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
items.description:
The sight that makes you sag

inside, just a little.

If you know, you know.

If soon it does get white, I'll have to think about decorations. Some Christmas-colored lights on the balcony, sure. A tree? I could get all-new decorations. Not sure what I kept, but they're packed away at Zork Storage. I like the idea of a clean install, since all the ornaments have stories and all the stories are dead.

Dry and cold.

Wrote a ton this morning, did a Substack, laid out three pages for next week, then off to the gym. Blue Oyster Cult was playing in the locker room, which made me smile, and also made me angry, recollecting the dinner we had with Buck Dharma and his wife one summer evening in Minneapolis, in the bygone life. Little triggers everywhere. Still warm enough for a post-workout walk down to Centennial Lakes, and at Birch's watering hole there was the fellow I ran into a few weeks ago, the Similarily Situated Recent Divorced Writer Guy. This was good, since I hadn't had a conversation with anyone  for a few days, and we swapped tales. I enjoy talking to people at length and the opportunities are few these days, so it charges all the batteries. Target to get dog-head meds, home for tea, nap. Fish-and-chips dinner with a spot of HP sauce, another packet liberated from the buffet at the Backrooms Hotel at Heathrow. Did the Aftershow with Duane, and then an evening of work. Two columns due tomorrow.

Anything else? Oh, always! So much more. Apparently I have to go into Discus tonight and ban another troll. I wonder what sort of mental energy it takes to tell yourself that everyone is struck to the pith of their marrow by your ripostes, when everyone either ignores or laughs. It's such a joyless, bilious existence, showing up under fake names and telling people to die.

Speaking of joy:

If you're a Substack subscriber, you recall this fellow from Wednesday, where I discussed the yin-yang attitude about hedonism in the 80s and 90s. The Captain was all about having big Rum Fun, but was obliged to shout "Responsibly!" now and then. You'll note his aides have banners that reinforce the idea. He's running for President because we're at the 2008 Democratic National Convention.

(I should note that the Wednesday entry is loosey-goosey, expanding on material removed from the Mon or Fri columns.)

Anyway, I was hanging around with a Miami Herald journalist who also had been sent to write humor, and we would shout "Responsibly!" at relevant intervals. I wondered if he remembered, so I wrote him last night. He did! We hadn't talked since his book about living with an old dog, which I enjoyed. He also noted with astonishment that he's about to turn 80.

I am not making that up.

Doesn't look a day over 58.

I was finishing some additions

to the 1980s TV ad section, and found this 1988 ad for Southern Comfort.  This was not an unusual plot or setting. The nostalgia for old classic American forms had been going on since

Happy Days

, but people still thought there were classic diners like this out there in the heartland, complete with Vic-Tayback types working the grill.

I don't think modern ads would choose "quit your job and go drinking" for the plot, but it worked back then.

Here's the shot I liked. You know itâs a real authentic Diner because thereâs a hardhat guy standing outside with his leg up on the bumper of his Ford pickup.

Let's see if we can upscale that a bit.

Not really.

I didnât read this is as a diner, though. Thatâs a gas station. It has the lines of a Moderne station, and you can read the left side as a hint of the bays.

Of course I had to find it. Googleâs AI was confident that it was in New Orleans, since thatâs what the ad was all about. Google AI was not correct. When I pressed a bit more, it said, with complete and total confidence:

This restaurant is actually not located in or around New Orleans at all.

While the commercial was produced to promote the New Orleans spirit of Southern Comfort, this specific scene was filmed at the iconic 66 Diner located at 1405 Central Ave NE, Albuquerque, New Mexico.

Oh! Great. Letâs take a look.

Remind me again how this is the super-intelligence that will conquer humanity

But wait. Letâs go to the dinerâs website. The history page says it burned down in 1995. The building above is a newer version. The old Diner was once . . . a gas station.

So is this how you spend you time

?

Yes, but it took five minutes. Then you do something else for the next five or ten, and at the end of the day you have all sorts of fun stuff rattling around your brain. It's not as if I'm going to overhear anyone saying "I saw that 1988 Southern Comfort commercial, and I just wish I knew the story behind those exterior location shots." But one can hope.

I bought online a nice old street clock, the type that used to stand on the corner on a pole like a streetlight. The online listing mentioned  a glowing dial. When I got it, I realized that it glowed because of radium, so this was a big mistake. I would have to dispose of it in pieces, surreptitiously. I was all the more irritated with myself when I remembered that I had bought one of these things before and had the same problem. How many radium-affected antique street clocks were there on eBay?

Mr. Felts. NARVEL Felts. I don't remember this one at all,

Wikipedia

:

Albert Narvel Felts (born November 11, 1938) is an American country music and rockabilly singer. Known for his soaring tenor and high falsetto, Felts enjoyed his greatest success during the 1970s, most famously 1975's "Reconsider Me".

It's a scant bio for a long career.

That will do. Hope you enjoyed the week! Substack up at 11 for paying customers, and we'll all meet here next Monday for more of the same, except completely different.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Thursday.
items.description:
The downpour abates,

and youâve a moment to dash out in the drizzle before the next rain-laden cloud lumbers over and opens up. All day, on and off. For the morning walk, a light mist that didnât deter Birch from his irrigations and deposits; after the gym, a certain sparkle in the air, like walking through effervescence.

We went down to the spot where he drinks -

-  and noted how much had fallen away.

Well,

I

noted. He noticed a dead squirrel and was intent on bringing it home. He contented himself with a stick at least six feet long, which he carried with the usual jaunty pride until it tangled in the leash,  then got between my legs and snapped in half. He looked at it:

oh itâs not as good now BUT itâs easier to carry so hurrah.

On we went, pausing every 15 seconds so he could bite the stick into smaller segments until it was no longer an object of interest, and was dropped and forgotten.

This was after the gym, which was no fun because

A)

the back has been screaming all day from yesterdayâs workout (as I have noted, I work out so I have a good explanation for the aches and pains of Advanced Age) and

B)

there's this little idiot who sets herself between a bench and the weight rack and does one exercise every nine minutes, spending the rest of the time tikking the tok. I finally said something today after she had stopped and I could replace my 30s:

âThis isnât a very good place to set up,â I said, gesturing at the weight rack. She gave me a blank look, pointed to her earbuds, and said something in Spanish and then went back to the critical visions on the phone. Sigh.

C)

The weird big guy who asked about Halloween Houses last week was in the locker room and started doing a dance to the song on the speakers. It was like watching a potbellied Frankenstein try to moonwalk. On the other hand, I got a hearty âhello Jamesâ from Mo and Alyssia, and itâs always nice to have someone say hello to you and say your name. Otherwise after a while you just float away and evaporate.

As for the rest of the day: O the boring things I could relate! And probably will!  I decided to iron all the sweaters and shirts, and arrange the closet for full-on  fall and certain winter. This made me feel absolutely no better about my closet than before, since the closets are the main flaw of Fred Base One. Thereâs no room for a bureau, so I have no drawers. Just fabric boxes and hangars. But at least things are neater and organized. Whew! Wipe the sweat from the brow and let the heart get down to resting rate after that! On to the next boring thing: fixing old websites. This usually means undoing previous bad decisions and making new bad decisions. But I shored up a lot of things, and was once again heartened by the quantity of material yet to be released. All for free!

Yeah, about that. Weâll get to that.

Dinner was the fifth meal Iâve gotten out of the Aldi 8-skewer marinated chicken pack ($7.99), and this pleased me to no end. Food is my greatest expense,  aside from all the regular recurring bills. Iâve started feeding the receipts into the Monarch money-management app, which totals everything up and breaks out the categories and says âyes, food is your greatest expense.â   Helpful. Finished with a lovely salad, then headed out for a walk in the drizzle. The three sisters are totally bare:

The evening has mysteries we will never know:

Back up to Fred Base One for the evening work. I stopped in the package room and saw a big box: ELECTRIC FIREPLACE. Fake, in other words. This was the sort of day that makes you want to stay inside and have a cup of tea and sit by the fire, if you had one, which of course I donât anymore. I I probably don't deserve one. It is entirely apt and symbolic of the Current Life that there are two fireplaces at the Fred, and neither produce any heat at all.

I donât know why I clipped this, but it provided an interesting prompt right away:

What? Australians?

That was

a British joke. Says the link:

The line was also used in Australia, in much the same context, although appearances of it in newspapers there post-date those in Britain and the USA.

The phrase was popularized by Tommy Trinder (1909-1989), a well-known and well-liked English comedian (seen here with Phil Silvers).

The article, it should be noted, does not have a picture of Trinder with Phil Silvers. The line with its parenthetical aside can be found in two other locations, neither of which have a picture of Phil Silvers.

I did find the picture, though.

About Mr. Trinder:

Thomas Edward Trinder CBE (24 March 1909 â 10 July 1989) was an English stage, screen and radio comedian whose catchphrase was "You lucky people!". Described by cultural historian Matthew Sweet as "a cocky, front-of-cloth variety turn", he was one of the United Kingdom's foremost entertainers during the Second World War.

Heeeeereâs Tommy!

All the bios seem to find this important, for a reason we'll get to in a moment:

In 1941, he appeared in

Eating Out with Tommy Trinde

r, a public information film promoting wartime British Restaurants.

Can we? We can:

The British Restaurants were a wartime experiment:

British Restaurants were communal kitchens created in 1940 during the Second World War to help people who had been bombed out of their homes, had run out of ration coupons or otherwise needed help. In 1943, 2,160 British Restaurants served 600,000 very inexpensive meals a day. They were disbanded in 1947. There was a political dimension as well, as the Labour Party saw them as a permanent solution to equalising consumption across the class line and guaranteeing a nourishing diet to all.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
items.description:
That was last week.

It's not like that anymore. It looked like this at Centennial Lakes, where I went to vote.

I was headed to the polling place when I noticed there was a polling place around the corner, in the Fire Station. Hmm. It's closer. This is probably it! I went inside, and told the lady my last name.

"James," she said, automatically. Okay well that's nice. She couldn't find me in the system, but I said I had moved - oh, well, you'll have to register. Fine! Over to the other table. Gave her my name. "Oh, I read you all the time!" she said. And that's nice too. I suppose my demographic was election judges, or people who could be, or admired them. If they're newspaper readers of a certain age, they might think well of Amy Klobuchar, running for Guber, because they read her father in the paper. I  like Amy, because I think she's old-school DFL / Nordic-model social compact / Wendy Anderson holding up a fish Minnesota liberal at odds with the DSA Metro surge, but I don't know if that particular ideological levee is made of concrete or sand. I disagreed with her father on a lot of things (not that he noticed or cared) and he was never particularly friendly when I ran into him on the radio station, but he did love Minnesota in that way we all did, once.

Anyway, the poll official couldn't get my address to take, and it turned out I was in the wrong place.

"But I'm just around the corner!" I said, adding "at the Fred!" Somehow Fred status was not enough. As it turned out this polling location was a temporary one, used by people who had gone to the Library before it was razed. The Library is about six blocks from Centennial Lakes, but I am not yet wise in the ways of Edina, so fine, no problem. Off to . . .

It was 1 PM, and empty. I voted, and was given a sticker. I always feel like I'm getting one of those balloons you got at the pediatrician that said "From My Doctor For Being Good" even if you'd screamed and cried when you got a shot. The man at the ballot-reading machine said "Thank you for voting," and I wanted to say "You're welcome! I wrote in Hitler for every office!" because voting's all well and good, but it does matter

what

you vote for, no?

Thank you for doing your part to advance every cause to which I am opposed with every molecule of my being!

But I get it. This is how we solve our problems, or at least produce a new group of officials who will take a different approach to not solving our problems.

I was watching that video of the raving student who attacked the Jewish student for noting wryly that her ordinary garb would not be popular in Islamic countries, and she was quite clear at the end in expressing her desire to kill the Jew, and heck, anyone else who's Jew-adjacent. If you're sufficiently online you see the

lol kys

a lot. These people do not thank you for voting.

Which brings us to the matter of the Bloody T-Shirt.                My feed has a series of headlines about the Minnesota Election Judge who was wearing a white shirt with a bloodstain. It was thought to be a reference to Charlie Kirk, and as such, some people were outraged. I'm not using the word lightly, since

everyone is always outraged

these days. It was later revealed that the judge was a Republican, and it was a Halloween T-shirt that's been around for a while. There was a

similar controversy in Tucson last year, this time concerning some math teachers.

I found the shirt for sale online, and it appears to preceded Kirk's assassination.

I'm not sure what the shirt is supposed to mean, except that the wearer has used violence to overcome a difficult situation. As far as I can tell, it's not a callback to some gory movie, or a reference to some quip in a book or a meme. It's just a bloody shirt with a phrase.

Interpreting it as a Kirk reference is entirely reasonable, though. If you saw all the Kirkiversary posts on X, or all the pictures people gleefully posted of themselves wearing white "Freedom" shirts with a bloodstain to indicate the bullet wound, of course that's what you'd think. I expect the old lady didnât know,  not being terminally online, but you can absolutely understand why someone would conclude it was one of innumerable happy recreations of Kirk's death.

The people who celebrate don't bother me as much as the people who wouldn't do it themselves, but, y'know,

kinda understand

why someone would?

Anyway. Wet day all around, no let up. A damp-dog-smell day. Gym, a bit of shopping, mindful of the new budget, no frills. Leftover Chicken Burger dinner for supper, absolutely delicious with Lundsnbyerly's Sriracha Mustard sauce and a big salad of spinach and something else that has a bitter taste so you say "it's not iceberg, must be healthy." I finished two projects I'd been picking away at all day, two 14-page websites on 40s culture. Now listening to swank French downbeat chill sung by some husky chanteuse who's been bruised by l'amour but is wiser for it. I think. She could be complaining about the historical trends in petrol prices, but probably not.

Ah: just translated the line she repeats, and it's "I don't remember taking  this path."

People say Reddit is a cesspool, and that's not quite accurate. There are many useful, factual, smart, reasoned subreddits. A lot depends on the moderators. You can tell a moderator has the cliched Reddit mindset when you see a rule like "4. Transwomen are women" and it's a subreddit devoted to fountain pens.

I was reading about the Paris riots in a subreddit devoted to Lost Architecture. As with 2020, you are sternly discouraged from mourning property destruction, which only shows you are missing the real issue.

Don't get me wrong, bro, I'm totally on board with burning museums, if they're the ones that need burning.

This one is fun, because it contains accusations of "state worship" from people who want to hand the state all sorts of sweeping powers, providing the state's objectives align with theirs.

Again, the reassurance:

don't get me wrong I totally understand burning down a building that has an office where people make money in a way that abrades my ideology, but City Hall?

This is the moderate view.

On X, the purest expression of the argument:

Of course the local resident and the city's money could be traced back to stolen colonial wealth, since that term has been redefined to encompass all money not yet in the hands of the State.

I also enjoy reading the local subreddits

to see how people frame and discuss current events. Nothing is ever surprising. You will have someone say something sane - always preceded by establishing bonafides:  âIâm a lifelong socialist and F Trump,â which means the arguments are meant in good faith, not from a PLACE OF HATE. This just means itâs generally ignored or quietly downvoted.

So: there was a big screaming mess at the Union Depot at The Bundle Halal Fall Event. Private party, lots of vendors, religious requirement for being a vendor. There was some sort of dispute that caused everyone to stampede for the exits. This slotted alongside the series of shootings around town at places and events not previously known for shootings, but if you note the rise in clan / gang warfare, youâre being jerked around by bots. The following replies are an almost perfect Reddit sequence:

The last one shifts the blame where all the right-thinking people know blame resides, so the matter is closed.

Elsewhere, in Dinkytown, a massive police presence. There have been many instances in the last few years when the police have had to flood into the neighborhood and break up late-night mobs of Youts who do not live in Dinkytown.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
items.description:
Dark and portentous day.

Rain from the start, mean rain, but not cold. You look out at the trees on the boulevard and realize theyâre all bare. Everythingâs bare. The curtain went down and the stage was reset.

I watched the storms on my weather app to see when thereâs be a break for Birch to do what he needed to do. Or, I could look out the window. When we went out in the drizzle there was no one around. The machinery wasnât running. Sunderwood Park has been completely churned up; all the grass and flora and weeds and such are plowed over, an dark sea of mud.

Did afternoon errands, and felt that I should be stockpiling, as the governments have been advising. It's amusing, because I used to have everything set aside for whatever emergency might beset the land. Turns out I was prepping for the wrong apocalypse. I still have dehydrated foods, but most of the Crisis Equipment went in the estate sale, I think. So I'm at Targe today, looking at sensible canned goods, like tinned chicken "in water," which I assume they have to add as a frank admission. You would never order chicken in a restaurant and ask the waiter "is that

in water

?"

Oh yes sir all of our chicken is in water.

I would never eat that stuff. I haven't room for serious supplies. I bought three packets of sriracha-infused tuna, which I use for sandwiches. I am woefully unprepared and feel uncomfortable about it.

Why? What's going to happen? Nothing is going to happen. Right?

In the evening

we went out between bouts of rain, and the same feeling persisted.  Strange unease on the margins. Half way down the block a series of pops! Sounded from the Seagate parking lot across the street, and Birch froze.

âDonât worry,â I said. âItâs not fireworks. Itâs just gunfire.â He wanted to make haste back to Fred Base One, and so we did. A neighbor from down the hall, Reed, was getting something from a car under the canopy, and he saw us and called out HELLO BIRCH!

We chatted about

the Mystery of the Footprints.

I saw this the other evening. Thick black muddy prints in the lobby. Who could be so careless?

Thick black muddy prints in the lobby. Who could be so careless?

Last night I noticed that the prints in the lobby were gone, but the ones in the garage remained.

I had the epiphany: these are going away from the apartment.

I followed the trail to the end of the parking garage.

Strange.

And then it got stranger. As I was walking back to Fred Base One, I saw the footprints in

my hallway

. They stopped

here

.

Theyâre turned away from the door because he was working the lock.

HOW DO YOU LEAVE YOUR HOUSE WITH TARRY SHOES

Anyway, based on my chat with Reed,

everyone is talking about this.

I found something in the unposted folder, filed away for later. It had that fatal combination of the intemperate and the irrelevant.

Trust me, I'm not going to nerd-rant. There's a point to all this. Anyway, I wrote:

You miserable juvenile legacy-trashing idiots

There is, in the history of

Star Trek

, no greater missed opportunity than Season 4 of

Strange New Worlds

. Aside from two or three solid episodes, it is a diminution of the  Trek series that aligns with

Discovery

, and highlights the inability of the writing and producing staff to understand the essence of thee great franchise.

Everyone acts like adolescents. Rom-com everywhere. Uhuru and Scotty are an item! But itâs on the down-low! Nevertheless Orteges, the shuttle pilot,.  sees them holding hands and makes a few remarks about it before she blasts off with Uhuru to take a shuttle into a black hole, and they talk about RELATIONSHIPS as they head into the BLACK FARGINâ HOLE, instead of acting like adults on a STARSHIP in the FEDERATION on a dangerous mission.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
items.description:
It is at the moment

11 on Saturday night, and I have fixed a  Manhattan. I used a blended Scotch. The bottle said âBottled in Scotland,â but that could mean they  ship huge vats of Chinese rotgut to some windswept village in the Hebrides, where flinty locals transfer the cheap hooch into bottles to earn the right to say it was bottled in the proper place. Itâs the only industry they have left since the fish stocks ran out. The town once had two pubs but one closed. The men wear thick gray turtlenecks and scan the horizon with long, empty stares. The children leave when they are grown.

There's nowt here but helpin' them steal the good name of the only thing we make that the world wants, Da! It's not honourable work!

IT PUTS FOOD ON THE TABLE! I'LL NOT HEAR A WORD AG'IN IT!

I have also cleaned the air frier, sullied by supper. I let it soak for a while, the procrastinatorâs trick.

Oh Iâd

love

to clean it now but I just canât, it has to soak.

I spent the night in the office working on three things, watching a somewhat rote 50s Noir that nevertheless kept my attention because of the charismatically malignant main actress; she put the lie to the whole Keats truth-beauty idea. (We will meet her below.) When it was done I went to refill my coffee, and there was the air frier in the sink, waiting to be scoured. So this I did.

Now the day comes down to doing the things I shouldâve done last night: topping off a successful interval of life with

Mobland

and ice cream,. I did not do the Friday tnings, because I made a mistake.  Felt a bit sentimental and in need of conversation, some catch-up-chit-chat. Anyone in my position knows what I mean. But: can I do that without getting sparky and finding the anger return and feeling all pathetic about that?

I finally stopped thinking about the mistake about 30 miles into Saturdayâs day trip to Lake City. Ninety minutes south along the border on a road Iâd not taken before.

This is a lake. It's also a river.

It's complicated.

Lake Pepin is a naturally occurring lake on the Mississippi River on the border between the U.S. states of Minnesota and Wisconsin. It is located in a valley carved by the outflow of an enormous glacial lake at the end of the last Ice Age. The lake formed when the Mississippi, a successor to the glacial river, was partially dammed by a delta from a tributary stream and spread out across the ancient valley.

I was headed down for lunch and convo with Painter Jean, an old friend who was the spouse with another fine Artist of the plains, Dave Matheny.

I worked with Dave at the paper. He was a man of particular talents, one of those rare individuals who can draw or paint wonderful brilliant work in different styles that were nevertheless instantly recognizable as his, and - this is where you narrow your eyes a bit and cast your glance at the heavens and say âyou

had

to give him

another

talent too, didnât youâ  - he was a natural writer, and quite funny. Normally âhumoristsâ hate each other on sight but we got along from the start. For a few years we were part of the same pod back in features: me, the FNG, Tom, the bald-headed bull - a former Marine - on copydesk; Neil, the TV critic; Bill, the sardonic copy editor who was also a gifted musician;  Dave, who had been done hard by the paper. For a long time heâd been the top illustrator, but styles had changed. Ccomputer graphics and photos were in vogue. Heâd been busted down to the Rail, writing "things to do this weekend" items and adding small delightful illustrations. It was like having Albrecht Durer on staff and making him ink Garfield.

He is gone. He is missed. Like Astrid curating her mother's work and memory, Jean is devoted to sorting and preserving the art he left behind, and thereâs a lot. When I move to the Last House I will take a few pieces - I have my eye on the drawing he did of my Close Personal Friend Sir Micheal Palin, when he interviewed the Pythons in New York. The paper used to have the money to send someone to New York to do such things. I am glad I saw the tail end of that era, and glad Dave got out before the collapse.

En route: Red  Wing, a storied town by the Bluffs. Very broad street for a small town:

This formation looks hairy and misshapen. Jabba the Bluff.

The strangest and most poignant building I saw, in Frontenac.

I found an older picture on Facebook, and colorized it. Honda and Lowenbrau:

Lake City reminded me, in a way, of Walbers - of course itâs one-ninth the age, and the architecture is different, but thereâs the great body of water  on the border, a restless realm.

Nice little downtown! New and Old.

I have no idea what someone was thinking when they decided to improve this Moderne facade. It looks like an alien vessel hovered overhead and attached some claws to pick up and take it away, but the locals fought it off.

When Jean talked about the village festival in the green, the local planning commission taking citizen input on paint choices for historic houses, I thought again of Walbers, and thought,

this is not a bad place to end up.

But I donât know what I would do there.

Then again, I donât know what Iâm going to do here. I mean, I do, every day:

Wake!

Breakfast!

Dog walk!

Website work until 10:30, edit Substack, update!

Lunch!

Scan and file!

in the elevator, lamenting the news. For three of them, he was the Professor. For me, he was the Captain.

He was perfect - arrogant, dissembling, flashing a false smile, scheming, and - spoiler - dying on the steps from wounds he most surely deserved. That was forty-six years ago. More on the matter on Tuesday, for reasons you will immediately understand. Part of a larger matter.

BTW, I saw the announcement on X, and I knew exactly what it meant, but I denied what I was seeing. I thought that Patrick Stewart was telling us to donate to Alzheimerâs research. Went to the page I used for general news. Sagged and sighed.

Back to the old neighborhood

today for another dog prescription. The usual irritation and disbelief. I mean, that's the strange emotion I get when I'm back:

disbelief I can't go home.

Otherwise, a carbon-copy day, proceeding through all the basics. Morning website work, write the Substack, post, lunch, dog walk to find the new poop place since everything's ripped up. Gym. In the locker room a very tall and heavy-set late-30s guy with black greasy hair said HELLO, and I said, hey. He asked about Halloween decorations in the neighborhood, and whether I'd put up any. I said I had not. He said, with a rather flat aspect, "no guts, no rotting torsos, no skeletons," and I said noooo, not in my part of Edina.

He wanted to know if there was a haunted house in Edina. A place where you go and, you know, it's full of Halloween. Did I know if there were any. I shrugged, trying not to look at the odd tattoo of bones and a eusophogus on his throat, and said he might try google, I don't know. I wasn't much of a Halloween guy myself.

Not a Halloween guy,

he said, looking away. Everything's going to be odd today, then.

Off to Target to drop off the scripts for Birch, and what's this? The staff is completely different. The very large pharmacist with the wig of rainbow hair and the upside-down crosses painted on the cheek is gone, and the head pharmacist, who has a heavy accent and always wears a mask and is thus somewhat difficult to understand, is gone. Everything

odd today.

what if we sold slippers? And what if dogs were  involved?

items.description:
More work

in Sunderwood Park. Today they tore up all the reeds around the Slough of Despond.

Sunny, and - I know, I know - short-sleeved shirt weather.

Last day! Never happen again!

Rumors of rain and tornados all day, with a gloomy front pushing in at suppertime. Not a day of great emotional vigor - Wednesday and Saturday are the days I have to get through. It takes extra effort to work, move, produce, and such. But I do it.

So pin a medal on

me

, I guess.

On the way back from errands I stopped at Infinite Intoxicants to get some vermouth. To show you how unskilled I am in the ways of cocktails, I didn't know vermouth was perishable. I had a huge bottle I'd bought for some party, and was certain it had gone over. I paused at the Blended Whiskys section, and one of the ever-helpful clerks came over to see if I wanted to try something. Anything. Why yes. I

do

believe I can find something to try. Do you have a bottle of the 30-year Skye open?

Back up:  year or two ago I noticed a new line of whisky on the shelves: Isle of Skye. It was offered, as they used to say, at Popular Prices. I tried a bottle, the entry level, was pleased, and added it to my rotation. Since then Iâve seen half a dozen other varieties come out. A special Cigar edition. A Smoky edition. A 17-year-old

intended to be sipped while studying the works of David Hume

edition. Thereâs a 30-year. Iâm always in awe of that sort of long game. Well, lads, letâs put it up and leave it, and come back in five years to start the 25 year old.

Who makes it?  I asked. The clerk he looked it up, and thereâs only one distillery on the island, and itâs Tallisker, so Isle of Skye could be sourced to that venerable brand. Huh! Who knew.

Well, I looked it up, and it's produced by Ian Macleod, a Scottish company with many brands. The companyâs website says Ian Macleod himself started making Isle of Skye in 1933.

Juuuuuust maybe the clerk was trying to give it a cachet it didn't earn, to see a bottle? It's possible.

âThis is new,â I said to the clerk. Hedges and Butler. It has an intentionally cluttered label, suggesting an ancient pedigree. Lots of kings.

The address, EH52 5BU, comes back to Broxburn. Letâs go to the street view!

I would guess thatâs

Roberto

.

Anyway, I said it might be one of those venerable brands with a long history someone bought and revived, and the current product has nothing in common with the whiskey King George enjoyed. If there was a specific recipe, you canât guarantee that the distilleries that provided the various parts of the blend are still around, or if theyâve kept the ingredients the same. So yes, itâs been reformulated, and itâs now made by . . . Ian Macleod.

Iâll try some on my next trip. By the way, I was looking at some Isle of Sky locations, far up north, areas with no towns of any great size, and saw a church  icon. Ah, let us look at some flinty old honest house of worship and tradition, keeping the ancient traditions alive on this sea-sprayed spit:

The reviews - and there are seven - say it is âa quiet place with no tourists.â

Another noted that the main thing to see was âcow hoof prints.â

It was built in 1810. Eventually there werenât enough people to maintain it, and it fell apart.

Anyway, I'm glad I noticed a new whisky, because now I'm thinking about that small ruin in an obscure part of Scotland, and wondering what happened. When the roof fell. When the walls toppled. What was the last hymn sung in that space? The last prayer?

This week's prompt. To tell you the truth, when I looked at the image in the folder, written and stored a year and a half ago, I wouldn't have been able to identify it without context.

I mean, it's just your basic demon, right?

No: it's as critical piece of popular culture history.

He SPOKE!

I didn't enjoy it all that much. I seem to remember it was a sloppy and uninvolving table. But another machine came along to the Valli shortly thereafter, and it was the greatest pinball machine of all time.

It has no equal. You might tout a machine that had some innovative  feature like MagnaSave, but thatâs a nice gimmick. You might make the case for the original 8-Ball - it sold more tables than Deluxe, for some inexplicable reason -  but youâd be wrong. Nothing had the combination of  skill shots and options like this one. It, too, spoke.

Whoops;

beaucoup D'Anglais

But who was the voice? It wasnât a synthesized voice, was it? Apparently it was. Not a digitized snippet, but a robot encouraging us to Chalk Up, and chiding us when we used Too Much English.

What was the first pinball machine? Some say (citation needed; who?) itâs

Baffle Ball

, but it had no bumpers or flippers.

items.description:
Last night I dreamt I went to Jasperwood again

.

Well actually no,

but I probably will tonight. Or rather this morning, since I go to bed after midnight. So tomorrow I will say "this morning I dreamed I went to Jasperwood again, but it was probably dark out when I was dreaming, so in away it was last night, inasmuch as the concept of 'night' is somewhat elastic, and depends on mood, the amount of light, whether you've gone to sleep or not, and so on." Anyway I'll work on that opening sentence, see what I can do.

POINT IS, I don't know where all my coats are, and which ones I gave away. Coats, parkas, jackets. I had about 16. Two winter parkas for the harshest days, for snowblowing duty. Many light spring / autumn jackets. different colors. She wanted me to do something about them long before the eviction, although I don't know if she demanded that I get rid of some. It was all a blur, anyway. Where would I go? Would there be room? Who knew? So I think I gave half of them to Goodwill. Now it's getting cold, and I have six jackets with the same weight.

This is why I cannot talk to her.

I should be able to walk to my closet in my house and get the proper coat. Thus I will dream tonight of walking up the steps to the front door and using my old key and turning left to open the doors of the beautiful hall closet and choose from a selection of coats I always took for granted.

I guess this was my problem. I always took my closet and my coats

for granted.

Stupid man.

The picture above is from Southdale, where I went to get a new jacket. That is the subject of Friday's column, because there was a moment that just stood up and waved a flag and said "Seven hundred words on this matter, no sweat." Southdale has now gone upscale, its latest overhaul. Looks nice, mostly full; not a lot of traffic. I used the loo on the lower level, the part that used to go to Al's Diner, and before that led to a subterranean concourse that certainly still exists, like walled-up catacombs. On the way I noticed something that made me sag a little bit, with sadness for the Bygone Things:

Looks like an 80s residue, but I believe it's from the 90s overhaul, back when the mall looked like this. (My photo.)

It's a style that aged out by decade's end, and everyone thought it looked weightless and gimcrack-baroque. Now it's the subject of sad nostalgic recollections on subreddits about malls and the 90s and

Global Village Coffeehouse aesthetics.

(This isn't GVC, but you know the bookstores and Starbucks abounded with the style.)

At least Southdale is still a going concern. I read today of a hotel in downtown Minneapolis that sold for, oh, $240 mil a while ago, and changed hands today for $5 million. Everyone in Minneapolis who owns a house will probably have to pay $4.27 to make up the lost tax revenue. I remember when it was built. It was a Radisson, so  it was pretty good.

It was good to go to the Mall and walk around. Rainy day, perfect place. But like downtown Minneapolis, there is an emptiness in the soul of the place. Southdale doesn't have that dead-and-forgotten downtown feel, but it's lost something, too. It was once so much livelier, and useful. I suppose I should be grateful it's still here.

Now and then I am reminded that I live a few blocks from the old Howard Johnson where my family stayed on our first trip to the Cities in the early 60s, and I just think . . . it's a bit too on-the-nose. I can see an editor saying "okay, well, what point are you trying to make?"

I don't know!

"That you can't go home again, but you can be caught equidistant between totemic architectural constructs that define a lost sense of post-war confidence and enthusiasm?"

Yeah okay maybe

In between bouts of rain,

we ventured out to note the changes in the world. New this morn: Big dig at Sunderwood.

There's no heading into the field anymore.

After the gym, we went to the lake. The man-made one. Something was different, and I noticed it right away.

The fountain in the middle of the lake is off. No more spray, no more ripples. All is calm.

Oh, one more thing:

on the evening walk, we saw two of the local turkeys. I think they're the last survivors.

It's possible they were struck by a car and forcibly transmuted into one turkey, but it's probably just the angle. From now on I will call these guys Doh and Dal.

Okay, another thing.

CHALLENGE TIME. There are two sentences in this Bleat that explain this image.

Find them.

Itâs 1925.

I'll bet the womenfolk hated being a "Burley Lady."

Well, let's see how different things were, so many years ago:

Yes, we have been hearing this over and over and over, and itâs never true. Might have been a production issue, though.

The bright lights of Hollywood lure another lad from the farm:

IMDB does not record his name. Sounds like he wouldâve been an extra in some oaters, uncredited. But the folks back home would go to the theater in hopes of a glimpse.

Theyâre still arguing about war debt.

Rain all day. At point it faded to drizzle, so we went out to Sunderwood Park to do what needed to be done. Ah: machinery on the move, terraforming.

Okay, I know I'm rehashing - sort of - a topic I was banging on about yesterday. And to repeat: I am not against the existence or usage of AI, but I am driven mad every day by the profusion of krep.

The world does not have to be ugly and the world does not have to be fake It is our obligation to oppse both conditions.

So:

This guy.

I hate that my first reaction is to doubt his existence, and then I'm glad I do. I saw an ad for this book somewhere, and everything about it, I mean

everything

struck me as AI. Itâs off in ways you canât quite describe, beginning with the title of the damned thing.

I asked AI if it was AI, and AI said it was AI. Over at Reddit they were debating whether the YouTubes associated with the âauthorâ were AI, given the number of videos released in a short period of time, the factual inaccuracies, and my favorite - mispronunciation of things a robot wouldnât catch. No, route 128 isnât pronounced âone hundred and twenty eight.â

"His" youtube webshite has the style I have come to loath with murderous intensity:

An American Icon - but there's darkness beneath the matronly cheer, because everything you knew is false and everything was horrible and sad and she was probably SA'd! (Can't say the words you know)

What, did they go rogue and sew women's sleeves to the desk so she couldn't leave the house?

Cities! Heat-resistent glass! Nothing you thought was true! Everything was really REALLY

dark

underneath

but now you know and you're smarter than everyone else who doesn't know how DARK Pyrex was

Also, you'll note that everything is "most impossible."

They sold it to MOST WOMEN who were IMPOSSIBLE TRAPPED in SUBURBIA!

It goes on like that forever. Tons of hour-long videos released within days of each other.

I donât log in to YouTube all the time, so I see the basic stuff it presents to the general population. Same thumbnail format: AI lettering, some guy making a shocked face, a red arrow, and some words about something was DESTROYED or FAILED or was the WORST. Itâs an infinite buffet of salty chum with several purposes: accumulating money and time and eyeballs, of course, But the unifying theme is the broken and empty state of the world. There is no point to doing anything. Everything is lame. Everything

ages poorly

.

The only things you can do: REACT, or EAT.

The latter is a popular topic, as we saw yesterday. I have never in my life wanted to seek out a series of moving images of someone eating. I don't know why anyone would. As for the former: there are innumerable videos of people reacting to some cultural creation, as if the act of responding means anything or communicates anything. It doesn't. Oh, it might make people feel superior (I knew about that a year ago and did my own reacting) or B) provide "relatable content" so we can be Just Like Our YouTube Friend before turning on them in a year for a petty reason, or C) give people the chance to adopt the reaction as their own, relieving them of the need to experience the thing themselves.

You could say that movie reviews in print did the same thing, I suppose, but with a review you have to look at words and process them into a thought; the reaction videos are just watching people pull faces and nod and dribble phonemes.

Again,

obviously

I'm not the target market.

I did watch, start to finish, without glancing at my phone, the Drinker's latest video on the Narnia movie. Tell me if anything about these pictures stands out.

The shot below is controversial, since she's not supposed to be able to do things, and the name of the pub was where Tolkein and Lewis met, and she destroys it, but that's not what I'm pointing out.

I despair. It's beginning to seem as if THE COLOR will never go away. I've been banging on about this for

years

.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
items.description:
For a week the mornings

have been cold, temps in the 40s - but then, after noon, the day thinks wait a minute, wait a minute, I can do better, and the warmth floods in on breezes that have none of autumnâs haughty chill. On Saturday it was in the 60s in the morning, and everything got brighter and hotter. Birch and I went to the lake and did the long walk, from which the image above was taken. Short sleeves again! Itâs a blessing. Itâs been a blessing all week, and we all knew this was the end.

True fall moved in around five and took the temps down ten degrees. Also around five the police showed up.

Okay, rewind. I was over at the Giant Swedeâs for a merry chili-fest that included the Crazy Uke and the entirety of his clever brood, and the Swedeâs kids were there as well, and a guest - like me, not related by blood or bonds. This was his first introduction to the particular verbal and intellectual and emotional pyrotechnics of the Swede-Uke Confluence, and itâs like tossing a match into a box of fireworks. Great fun. All the rituals were observed before the meal: a shot of vodka and the Lordâs Prayer, everyone in a circle, holding hands. Iâd brought Birch, and he decided that the group chant was the perfect time to start barking, and as we tried to drown him out by raising our volume, he barked louder. Adorable. Everyone there loves dogs, so thereâs that.

The police came because four Youts from down the street had walked through the alley, thought it would be fun to pick up a piece of wood that had a nasty 16â spike driven through it, and throw it over the Swedeâs garage. It bonked the Uke's daughter on the dome, and lucky for her - if you can put it like that - she wasnât speared with the rusty nail, so thereâs that.

It takes a certain type of sociopathy to pick that up and throw it towards the sound of people conversing and laughing.

The Giant Swedeâs ex-wife, to the surprise of no one, chased after them, but they lolâd and loped away. The police were called. Since no one could be found, no report was made because nothing happens in situations like this. They just keep their eyes peeled for four youths walking through alleys, and then let them pass because theyâre not spearing people with pieces of retaining wall

at the moment.

I had my chili outside on the patio in shirt sleeves, even though it was now in the minor 60s. Birch was more or less good, since there was food about and he could leverage his charisma to get some. At one point he barked in a way that indicated he was overloading, so I took him out across the street to walk and mark. Thereâs a classic mid-century structure, the sort of featureless building that nevertheless says elementary school. I am not quite certain why its most prominent vertical feature is an incinerator.

\

Talked to the new guy about movies, top faves, etc. He mentions he liked War of the Worlds, and had been terrified when he was it on video because he was, you know, ten. SIGH. I asked if heâd seen the original, and he didnât know there was one. I do not hold this against anyone. I have come to expect that even the brightest youths interesting in movie and arts do not have a cultural literacy that goes past 1978. The best and smartest have, at least, an understanding of the

shape

of things, and perhaps have seen the seminal films. They can talk about the studio system and the rise of the young directors in the 70s. But I find it hard to convince them to watch old movies. Old in my sense. Thereâs always something new and fun and shiny, and I understand: one watches the products of oneâs time. But thereâs so much that just languishes in the dark unwatched, and eventually its tropes and faces and sounds and styles ebb away into nothingness.

On the other hand, the odd cultural status of the 21st century -  the way nothing really seems to change  - means that

War of the Worlds,

the Spielberg version, doesnât seem dated at all, even though itâs (sigh) 21 years old. Even in 1977 the 1953 War seemed to be from another era.

The good news: there are people who love the old movies, and will use AI to make new 1940s noirs. And theyâll be interesting, because they will have directors who are making intentional choices. Someoneâs going to make the

Maltese Falcon

sequel. I mean,

the scriptâs right there.

Iâm not opposed to this.

BTW, the link has an image to another Falcon sequel, which Iâd forgotten about. Itâs supposed to be bad. It has Elisha Cook Jr. and Lee Patrick - the original movieâs secretary - reprising their role.

Take a look at the poster.

This was intended to make you think of . . .

This, of course.

But what was

The Sting poster

Ordinary day in every respect. A dupe of the day before, except I went to Aldiâs, the place that doesnât bother to provide shopping baskets. They think youâll want a cart. I donât want a cart. I donât have a quarter deposit on me and I donât want to carry one around, just in case I go to Aldiâs. Itâs like asking me to secrete a doubloon in the arch of my shoe in case I want to drop in at the tavern and have an Armanac. Yes it is EXACTLY LIKE THAT. Now, if Aldiâs was more interesting, like the British Aldiâs, Iâd be there weekly, and I would have a special quarter in its own little holder, in the glove compartment, but since I donât go often, I have to carry everything in my hands.

Or use my shopping bag. This feels like youâre shoplifting. Iâm walking around putting things in the bag,  and things should only be in the bag after they have been redefined as mine by the process of beeping. So I put everything in the bag, go to the register, take everything out of the bag, beep it, put it back in.

The other day at CUfB I was beeping a pizza for the Sunday get-together, and was suddenly aware of a presence next to me. It was an old lady holding a four pack of toilet paper. She said âCan you help me.â Flat voice, a bit demanding. Didnât make eye contact. I said sure, although I didnât know exactly what she wanted. I turned the package around until the bar code was showing and said, there you go, thatâs what you scan. She handed me her credit card. âCan you do it.â

Uh - well I guess sure

But by now the attendant she had called was over, and the employee helped her. I gave her back her card. It was a credit card from Scheelâs, of all places. Scheelâs , the Fargo hardware store that got big. Now they sell sporting equipment and guns and tents and such. I had the sudden conviction that her husband got the card five years ago, but he was gone now, and it was the card she used because it was the card she used.

When I got outside I saw her get into the passenger side of a car idling in the handicapped, and wondered why the driver couldnât have helped Mom, you know? Donât you know? Canât you tell?

The more I consider The Last House the more I realize that I will be scouring away more and more to reduce any remnants of the old life. This, I regret. But. The thing I donât like about my office now are the sad shelves of books and collected items. The books and items are important, but the shelves - two where once there were ten - are a pallid and pathetic remnant of my old office. It used to feel like a cultural repository. Hell it WAS exactly that. Now most of it is boxed up, aside from the few items I gave away. I laugh every Sunday I got to the Giant Swedeâs and see the item I gave him, because I was downsizing, you know!

Well no, that wasn't it.

The thought of the next place gives me the opportunity to lavish time and attention on the most quotidian concerns. Right now I have a set of dishes and silverware appropriate for one man. A Target set. Four big plates, four small, four bowls. The silverware has 8 forks (two sizes) 8 spoons (two sizes) and four knives. This means I have to run the dishwasher every other day. I hate the dishwasher; the door is flimsy, unlike the sturdy Bosch I had when I was a landed man. It would be a waste of my finite resources to buy a solid dishwasher if I move to a house, but I will. It would be a waste of finite resources to replace the hated stove with something better. But I will.

Or will I?

After all, Iâm cheap. I live my financial life with the lines in my finance app always in the back of my head. Let the red neâer soar above the blue. When I shop for food, I will forswear an item if itâs not on sale and I know it will be soon. This is probably pound-foolish behavior, but I am gladdened when I look back on a day and think âI did not spend a sou.â What makes me think Iâll walk into Best Buy and say âThe top-of-line-Meile dishwasher, my good man, and hang the expenseâ like some tosspot young aristo just bounced from college for gambling debts?

I think I will have to rely on my friends. They will have to take me out for dinner and fortify me with spirits - a shot or three of Icelandic Aquavit. Then they take me to the store and call over a sales associate and say âour friend here has had a bad patch. Wife left him. Had to sell his house and leave his neighborhood. Before that he had his career yanked out from under his feet -â

âI dint get fired I took thâ buyoutâ I slur. âThey kild my column becush they were bean-counter bastiches who cudânât see I was big in print. I WUSH BIG IN PRINTâ

âSee? Heâs still dealing with things. What he needs is some top-line appliances. Well not toppermost of the poppermost if you know what I mean. But solid and sturdy with a good brand.â

Then I wake the next morn with a pounding head and three AMEX notifications.

All of the kitchens I see in potential houses have microwave ovens built into the stove area. This will be another area of concern. I hate my microwave right now. Hah: look at that. Look at that, what I just said.  My microwave. Itâs not! Itâs theirs! Itâs ALL THEIRS!

What I hate about the microwave is the same thing I detest about the Hated Stove, the cheap membrane keypad, the unresponsive controls, the flimsy door. When I think of these things I think of the LG microwave I had at Jasperwood, how well I knew its quirks, how it had dials and knobs. The way the finish had come off the knob after 15 years, but I knew how to finesse that dial -

And now, on schedule, the same old got-damned emotion returns. Iâm describing home. Iâm going back soon, right?

Iâm not going home?

What the hell

Why am I HERE

How the hell did

that

happen

Where is my big tree where is my fence where is my shed where is my back gate where is my house

DING!

Ahhh crap, new mail from Ex.  She acknowledges receipt of the pin for transferring her phone off the shared account. The last filament severed.

Does she still owe me for the last few months? Did I forget that she paid in advance? Will she be mad if I bring it up?

Anyway. Resolution: NEW PLATES from CRATE AND BARREL, NICE ONES. A proper sturdy Cuisinart toaster to replace this flimsy burninator I have now. New placemats, new napkins. Everything from Fred Base One will probably go in the finished basement, if there is one. Hey, it's 1973! I'm dad!

But if the kitchen was untouched 1962? Tempting. The cupboards in my Fargo home were light wood with modernistic copper handles. Just beautiful. Start again, again. Target date for the last reinvention: April, at the latest. Birch and I will walk out of here with purpose and joy some early spring day, or perhaps a late raw March when everything is brown and empty. It will feel odd:

I will wonder if I accomplished anything of note, and conclude that I had done my work and I had not shirked or slackened.

Two columns to file, then radio, then hallelujah! Done! Nothing but delights ahead. After the gym we walked to the shore at Centennial, and I listened to The Rest is Historyâs interview with an art historian about Jacques-Louis David, one of my favorite painters. Classic example (sorry) of having to distinguish the artist from the art. I learned something I didnât know, which is always good. Consider these two:

You may know the couple. Mr. & Mrs. Lavoisier. Scientists.

Consider their work:

Lavoisier is noted for his discovery of the role oxygen plays in combustion, opposing the prior phlogiston theory of combustion. He named oxygen (1778), recognizing it as an element, and also recognized hydrogen as an element (1783).

By using more precise measurements than previous experimenters, he confirmed the developing theory that, although matter in a closed system may change its form or shape, its mass always remains the same (now known as the law of conservation of mass), which led to the development of the balanced physical and chemical reaction equations that we still use today.

Lavoisier helped construct the metric system, wrote the first extensive list of elements, in which he predicted the existence of silicon, and helped to reform chemical nomenclature. (1787)

His wife and laboratory assistant, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, became a renowned chemist in her own right, and worked with him to develop the metric system of measurements.

Her individual bio's impressive, too.

Remarkable people. The intellectual vanguard of a sophisticated, inquisitive culture.But that culture changed with remarkable speed and ferocity.

At the height of the French Revolution, he was charged with tax fraud and selling adulterated tobacco and was guillotined despite appeals to spare his life in recognition of his contributions to science. A year and a half later, he was exonerated by the French government.

The painting was never shown in public. Itâs at the Met now, which is where I saw it a few years ago. Her dress, the rendering of the scientific equipment - itâs exquisite. What I learned today was not that David painted them; I knew that. What was news was the extent of Davidâs political activity. (Iâd read Citizens, but forgot about it.) David, as a member of the Committee,

signed Lavoisierâs death certificate.

I think this is the only instance in the history of art where the portrait painted contributed directly to the death of his subject.

He had a remarkable life, knew when to trim the sails to catch the wind from another direction, and died at 77 - when he was run over by a carriage.

. The best part: videos of these horrid things being delivered and rated, so you can see the target market. These people have no taste. There was never any reason to have taste. They don't know what they don't know and they don't care because if they don't know it, it doesn't matter.

The lurid profusion of this garbage means it'll burn out quickly, I think.

But I said that about The Color in TV advertising.

Half price round-up!

The market for zero-sugar Oreos was not as predicted. I'd never heard of them. I was not tempted. Oreos just seem like fake-choco-chalk to me now.

Ritz tried a brand extension. I gather it was not met with bright-eyed excited glee from the target market. OUTTA HERE

Some dark part of myself of wich I am not proud is always happy to see overprised pretentious coffee go teats up

One of those trends that infected many products: HOT HONEY. I've never been tempted.

Summer's over, I guess: bubble wands and S'mores caddies (great idea but a lot to schlep if you're camping) are marked to go.

I never saw any of these things in the store. I don't even know where they would be, and I know that store intimately.

I was supposed to do standup for the newspaper on a television channel, and I was auditioning, but I had completely forgotten my entire routine. Somehow, I could never find the right Zoom room in order to deliver it and there didnât seem to be anybody there anyway, but I kept getting phone calls from people of the paper telling me how happy they were that I was coming back and doing stand-up. Eventually, I left and drove somewhere to a meeting , canât quite remember the purpose of rationale, but I was in a Jeep and we went to the top of a hill, and stopped, and Telly Savalas got in the car and wanted to know if I wanted a special basket of fruit from his wife because she wanted to give it to me.

(Note: this dream's origins come from the time in 1994, poolside in LA, when Telly called me over because he wanted to talk about my laptop.)

Says the YouTube description:

This is the award winning video from Luis Cardenas, the gregarious and talented drummer from Renegade. This incredible video features Luis and his record breaking drum set, animated dinosaurs, Donny Osmond, Del Shannon and famed publicist Norman Winter.

Oh well if Norman's there, count me in

He's a drummer, so he has to run around drumming on things.

According to the comments, the cop . . . is Del Shannon.
